body_markdown:
Have you ever come home from the grocery store with a big bottle of ketchup, only to discover you already have two in the pantry? The easiest way to stop buying groceries you already have is to[organize your food](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/keep-your-kitchen-organized-and-stop-wasting-food.html) so you can see what you’ve got, check your supplies before shopping, and keep a running grocery list. You don’t need an elaborate inventory system, either. A few small changes to how you store food and shop can save you money, reduce food waste, and keep your kitchen from getting cluttered.


## Key takeaways


- Check your pantry, refrigerator, and freezer before making a grocery list so you don’t buy things you already have.


- Group similar foods together so you can see how much of each item you have.


- Keep a running grocery list and add items as you run low instead of trying to remember everything on shopping day.


- Put newer groceries behind older ones so you use what you already have first.


- Create a designated spot for backup groceries so you don’t accidentally buy extras.


- Use clear containers, baskets, or labels to make food easier to find.


- Plan meals around ingredients you already have before buying more groceries.


## Group similar groceries together


One of the easiest ways to prevent duplicate purchases is to give each type of food a designated spot. Instead of scattering cans, boxes, and bags wherever they’ll fit, group them into categories.


For example:


- Pasta and rice


- Canned vegetables


- Canned beans


- Soups and broths


- Baking supplies


- Breakfast foods


- Snacks


- Condiments and sauces


- Spices and seasonings


- Oils and vinegars


- Baking mixes


- Drinks


You don’t need to buy a bunch of organizers to do this. Just keeping similar items on the same shelf can make a big difference. The goal is to make it easy to glance into your pantry and see whether you already have what you need.


## Organize your refrigerator


The refrigerator can be just as bad as the pantry when it comes to duplicate groceries. It’s easy to buy another tub of sour cream when the one you already have is hiding behind a carton of milk.


Try organizing your refrigerator into zones. Keep similar foods together and avoid packing shelves so tightly that you can’t see what’s in the back. You can also use clear bins to group smaller items, such as yogurt cups, cheese, and packaged snacks.


Don’t forget the door shelves. Check for duplicate condiments, salad dressings, sauces, and other bottles before buying more.


## Don’t forget your freezer


Freezers are notorious for hiding food. That bag of frozen broccoli you bought six months ago may be buried underneath frozen pizzas, leftovers, and a bag of mystery meat. Start by taking inventory of what’s inside. Group similar foods together so you can find them without digging through everything.


You might organize your freezer into categories like:


- Frozen vegetables


- Frozen fruit


- Meat and poultry


- Seafood


- Frozen meals


- Bread and baked goods


- Leftovers


- Desserts


If you have a chest freezer, baskets can help keep food from getting buried at the bottom.


Label homemade meals and repackaged foods with the contents and date. Otherwise, you may end up buying more of something because you can’t remember what’s inside that frozen container.


If you have a large freezer, keeping a list of what’s inside can save you a lot of time. You don’t need anything fancy. A dry-erase board on the freezer door or a note on your phone can work just fine.


Write down what you have and cross things off as you use them. If you have several packages of the same food, include the quantity.


For example:


- Ground beef: 3 packages


- Chicken breasts: 2 packages


- Frozen broccoli: 4 bags


- Frozen strawberries: 1 bag


- Homemade chili: 3 containers


This is especially helpful if you buy meat in bulk, freeze leftovers, or stock up on frozen foods when they’re on sale. Just remember to update the list. An inventory that hasn’t been touched in six months probably isn’t going to help much.


## Check your groceries before making a shopping list


Before you start writing down what you need, take a quick look through your pantry, refrigerator, and freezer. Check the ingredients you use most often, along with anything you need for meals you’re planning to make. This little habit can prevent a surprising number of duplicate purchases.


You don’t have to count every can and box. Just make sure you’re not buying something you already have plenty of. If you’re planning spaghetti for dinner, for example, check for pasta, sauce, and any other ingredients before adding them to your list.


## Keep a running grocery list


Trying to remember everything you need while walking through the grocery store is a good way to end up with things you don’t need and forget the things you do. Instead, keep a running grocery list and add items as you notice you’re running low.


You can use:


- A notepad on the refrigerator


- A magnetic grocery list


- A notes app on your phone


- A shared grocery list app


- A whiteboard in the kitchen


- A voice assistant that supports shopping lists


The best system is the one you’ll actually use.


If you live with other people, a shared list can be particularly helpful. Everyone can add items as they run low, which makes it easier to avoid buying something another person already picked up.


If several people in your home buy groceries, duplicate purchases can happen even when everyone has good intentions. One person buys bread on the way home from work, while someone else grabs another loaf during their regular shopping trip.


A shared grocery list can help, but communication matters, too. If someone picks up something on the list, they should mark it as purchased or remove it. You can also agree on who usually buys certain groceries or handles the main shopping trip.


## Check the list before you leave


Even if you keep a running grocery list, take a minute to double-check it before heading to the store. You may have added milk three days ago, but someone else bought some yesterday. Or maybe you put flour on the list and then discovered an unopened bag in the back of the pantry.


Walk through the list and check anything you’re unsure about. Cross off items you already have enough of.


## Take pictures of your pantry and fridge


If you frequently find yourself standing in the grocery store wondering whether you have enough pasta sauce, try taking a few pictures before you leave. Snap photos of your pantry shelves, refrigerator, and freezer so you can check them while shopping.


This won’t work perfectly if your shelves are packed and you can’t see everything, but it can be a quick way to avoid buying duplicates without keeping a detailed inventory. You can also take pictures of specific areas, such as your spice cabinet or baking supplies, if those are the things you tend to buy twice.


## Plan meals around what you already have


Before planning meals for the week, look at what’s already in your kitchen. Maybe you have a bag of potatoes that needs to be used, several cans of beans, or frozen chicken you bought last month. Plan a few meals around those ingredients instead of starting with an entirely new grocery list.


For example:


- Have extra rice? Plan stir-fry or rice bowls.


- Have several cans of beans? Make chili, soup, or burritos.


- Have frozen vegetables? Add them to pasta, casseroles, or soups.


- Have a lot of eggs? Plan omelets, breakfast sandwiches, or a frittata.


- Have extra pasta? Make spaghetti, pasta salad, or baked pasta.


This can help you use food before it goes bad and keep your grocery bill from growing unnecessarily.


## Stop buying things just because they’re on sale


Sales can be great, but only if you’re buying something you’ll actually use. If you already have four jars of peanut butter, buying three more because they’re on sale may not be the best use of your money or pantry space.


Before stocking up, ask yourself:


- Do I already have plenty of this?


- How quickly will my household use it?


- Will it stay good until we use it?


- Do I have somewhere to store it?


- Is the sale price actually a good deal?


If you know your family goes through a lot of a particular food, buying extras may make sense. Just make sure you’re not buying more than you can reasonably use.


## Check your spices before buying more


Spices are one of the easiest groceries to buy twice because the containers are small and often get lost in cabinets. Before shopping for a recipe, check your spice collection. You may already have the cumin, paprika, or cinnamon you need.


[If your spice cabinet is packed, try organizing it](https://publicstorage.blog/organizing/how-to-organize-spices-when-you-have-too-many/) with tiered shelves, a turntable, or small baskets. Label the tops of bottles if you store them in a drawer. Keep duplicate spices together so you can see how much you have before buying more.


## Keep your grocery storage from getting cluttered again


Once you’ve organized your food and created a shopping routine, try to keep things from getting out of control again.


A few small habits can help:


- Put groceries in their designated spots when you get home.


- Move older food toward the front when adding new packages.


- Check your pantry before making a grocery list.


- Update your freezer inventory when you add or remove food.


- Keep backup groceries together.


- Check for duplicate spices and condiments occasionally.


- Use open packages before starting new ones when possible.


- Plan meals around food you already have.


- Go through your pantry, fridge, and freezer regularly.


You don’t need to spend hours organizing groceries every week. A few minutes of checking what you have before shopping and putting things away can make a big difference.


## FAQ


### How do I stop buying groceries I already have?


Start by organizing your pantry, refrigerator, and freezer so you can easily see what you own. Check your food before shopping, keep a running grocery list, and group backup items together. A simple inventory can also help if you have a large pantry or freezer.


### What is the best way to organize groceries to prevent duplicates?


Group similar foods together and give each category a designated storage spot. Use baskets, clear containers, or labels to make items easier to find. Keep older groceries toward the front and store unopened backups in one area.


### How do you keep track of what’s in your pantry?


You can use a written inventory, a notes app, or a simple list taped inside your pantry door. If you don’t want to track every item, focus on foods you frequently buy twice, such as pasta, canned goods, spices, and baking supplies.


### How do you avoid buying duplicate groceries when shopping with a partner?


Use a shared grocery list that both people can update. Mark items as purchased when someone buys them, and check your pantry and refrigerator before shopping. Agreeing on who handles certain shopping trips can also help prevent duplicate purchases.


### How do you keep track of food in your freezer?


Make a list of what’s inside your freezer and include quantities for foods you keep in bulk. Update it as you add or use items. Group similar foods together and label frozen leftovers with their contents and dates.


### Is buying groceries in bulk a good way to save money?


It can be if you regularly use the food, have room to store it, and can finish it before quality declines or it spoils. Buying more than you need can lead to wasted food and clutter, even if the price per ounce is lower.


### How often should you clean out your pantry?


Give your pantry a quick check every few weeks to look for duplicates, spills, and foods that need to be used. A more thorough cleanout every few months can help you catch forgotten items and keep shelves organized.


### How can I reduce food waste and save money on groceries?


Check what you already have before shopping, plan meals around existing ingredients, use older food first when it’s safe, and avoid buying more than your household can reasonably eat. Keeping your pantry, refrigerator, and freezer organized makes it easier to use groceries before they go to waste.
